newsitem.title: GERMANY: German DAX mounts 2,900 points for first time ever.
newsitem.headline: German DAX mounts 2,900 points for first time ever.

text.p: Germany's DAX index of leading shares stormed higher on Tuesday and ended electronic dealings above 2,900 points for the first time ever, after the dollar soared to a 23-month high against the mark.
Strength in German government bonds, also at record highs, provided additional support for the market.

The IBIS DAX, measuring all-day computerised dealings in the DAX index of 30 leading shares ended up a massive 1.66 percent, or 47.30 points at 2,900.76 points, touching to an all-time high of 2,901.26 points before the close.
Earlier the DAX index closed floor trade at 2,886.98 points, marking a gain of 28.38 points, or 0.99 percent, its fourth record close in a row.
Dealers said the rally was not over yet, although most analysts' year-end targets had already been reached.
"We've had a huge run, but we remain bullish. Some investors had been holding back, but now they are being forced into the market," said one trader.

The U.S. currency rose above the crucial 1.56 mark level overnight following comments by Bundesbank chief economist Otmar Issing and New York Federal Reserve Bank William McDonough on the dollar becoming more important in the run up to European monetary union.
Dollar strength benefited the German export-oriented chemicals and auto maker sectors in particular.
Shares in carmaker BMW AG gained most in IBIS trade, ending up almost six percent, or 59.30 marks, at 1,075.90 marks.
Dealers said dollar strength had helped the stock and also sterling firmness, because of the firm's Rover operations in Britain.
Shares in chemical companies Bayer and BASF both gained five percent, Bayer rising 3.18 marks to 65.55 marks and BASF 2.88 marks firmer at 60.88 marks.
Meanwhile, shares in Europe's largest car maker Volkswagen AG ended up 4.50 marks at 597.50 marks, as bargain hunters moved in to buy shares at lower prices.

In early dealings the stock had dropped over three percent to 574 marks, after a U.S. judge denied the firm's motion to dismiss General Motors Corp.'s remaining industrial espionage claims against the German carmaker.
